- **2026-09-13** [Propagating Ashitaba (Angelica keiskei) — Division, Seed, and the Monocarpy Problem](home/research/agent-reports/2026-09-13-ashitaba-propagation.md)
  - Q: How do you propagate ashitaba (Angelica keiskei)? Can it be cloned vegetatively, and if so how? Plus life cycle, seed handling, and conditions for Austin zone 8b/9a.
  - Crown division is the only home-viable clone route (Feb at bud-break, or Oct-Nov; cut through the crown so each piece gets buds AND roots; for a single plant, halve it in place rather than lifting). Stem cuttings do not work for the genus. THE BIG ONE: A. keiskei is functionally monocarpic — it flowers at 3-4 years and dies — but PFAF states it is reliably perennial IF prevented from setting seed, so deadheading every bolt is a survival requirement, not tidiness. Heat triggers bolting, so August is the watch window; Tokyo's island research center documents lowland summer production failing and moved the crop to 400m. Afternoon shade mandatory in Austin. Seed is short-lived (sow within the calendar year, 'torimaki'), light-requiring (surface sow, no cover), wants ~15C, and emerges unevenly over ~30 days. Alkaline limestone is fine — sources lean neutral-to-weakly-alkaline. No US extension literature and no peer-reviewed propagation paper exists for this species; best tier is Japanese horticultural media plus one Tokyo Metropolitan research center. Root cuttings and layering are genuine evidence gaps.

- **2026-09-13** [Vegetative Propagation from Zero — Equipment, Technique, and a First Project (Austin 8b/9a)](home/research/agent-reports/2026-09-13-propagation-setup-and-technique.md)
  - Q: What equipment does a complete beginner need to propagate plants vegetatively, and what is the underlying technique? Targeted at cloning creeping lemon thyme cultivars, dividing ashitaba, and seed-starting chamomile/savory/frogfruit in Austin.
  - Tier A is ~55 dollars and is genuinely all that's needed: trays, coarse perlite + coir, bypass snips, razor blades, bleach/alcohol, spray bottle, labels. TAMU's own herb publication propagates thyme/sage/savory in moist sand in shade in 4-8 weeks with no dome, no mat, no hormone. THE COUNTERINTUITIVE ONE: a humidity dome is the WRONG choice for thyme and other small-leaved resinous or grey-fuzzy plants — they transpire little and rot readily, so run the system DRY; a dome plus heat mat is the single most reliable way to kill a thyme tray. Heat mats are counterproductive whenever ambient is already at target (most of the Austin year), and an unregulated mat sits 10-20F above ambient, landing near 95F root zone; if you buy a mat the thermostat is mandatory, not optional. Thyme does not need rooting hormone — it roots on endogenous auxin; if buying, Garden Safe TakeRoot at 0.1% IBA is exactly the right spec (herbaceous/softwood range is 500-1250 ppm = 0.05-0.125%), and Hormodin 3 / Hormex 16-45 / Clonex are 3-45x too strong (excess auxin promotes callus and hinders rooting). Willow water, honey, aspirin and cinnamon are unsupported; the willow-contains-IBA claim is chemically wrong (salicylates, not indoles). BIGGEST STRATEGIC FINDING: Missouri Extension names LAYERING, not cuttings, as 'the simplest and most reliable method' for thyme, lemon balm, winter savory, sage, bay and rosemary — and mound/stool layering is the highest-multiplication lowest-equipment route for a self-rooting subshrub. EXPECTATION SETTER: one 3-inch pot yields only 10-25 cuttings or 3-5 divisions, so it becomes dozens in TWO steps over about a year — realistic joint plant-out is fall 2027, and the way to compress it is buying more pots now, not more equipment. June-September is a hard no-propagation, no-plant-out window in Austin. Legally, a falsifiable patent search (positive control: 123 hits for Lavandula) found NO patented Thymus cultivars, but note there is no personal-use exemption in 35 USC 163 — home propagation of a patented plant is unenforced, not permitted.

  - Mail-order thyme is in a fall stock trough: all seven High Country Gardens creeping thyme cultivars are out of stock (fall ship window for zones 7-8-9 opened Sept 28), and Mountain Valley Growers' plug trays are out for the small-leaf cultivars that matter ('Elfin', 'Pink Chintz', Mint). Locally, It's About Thyme — named twice in plant-sourcing.md as the first call for bay laurel and herbs — has been CLOSED SINCE SUMMER 2018. - **2026-09-12** [Joint-Viable Repellent Groundcovers — Full Candidate Set, and Whether Any of It Works on Ticks and Chiggers](home/research/agent-reports/2026-09-12-joint-repellency-candidates-ticks-chiggers.md)
  - Q: Considering every anti-mosquito plant, which ones can actually serve as flagstone joint groundcover in Austin, and do any of them also deter chiggers and ticks?
  - Of the four plants the corpus found actually work on mosquitoes (mountain mint, catnip, lemon thyme, bee balm), exactly ONE — lemon thyme — is small enough to live in a joint. The other three are perimeter plants, and whiteleaf mountain mint is on the Wildflower Center's October sale list, so the missing layer is buyable now. The joint-viable + documented-chemistry + non-toxic set is small: lemon thyme cultivars (citral + thymol), the plain creeping thymes (weaker, cultivar-dependent), creeping oregano and creeping savory (carvacrol, chemotype-dependent). Pennyroyal would outperform all of them and stays banned on toxicity; Corsican mint carries the same pulegone and should fall under the same rule. On TICKS the compound evidence is strong — thyme oil repelled 100% of lone star tick nymphs within 15 min at 10 ug/cm2, the most active of 16 oils tested — but that study states plainly that no living plants were tested. On CHIGGERS there is no plant evidence at all; Texas A&M AgriLife recommends habitat change plus DEET/sulfur/permethrin. The patio itself is the chigger and tick intervention: dry, sunlit, hardscaped, low-humidity ground is hostile habitat by construction.

  - Alma (Honey) and Celeste (Sugar) are adjacent groups on the same sweet/low-acid half of the map — the current pair is one flavor at two seasons. The flavor jump with the least added risk is Violette de Bordeaux (Bordeaux/resin-berry group: closed eye, documented rain resistance, naturally semi-dwarf, sold as a rooted tree by Bob Wells TX and Ison's GA). Smith/Texas BA-1 and Violette de Solliès are the higher-ceiling options; Solliès has an Austin grower rating it above Black Madeira for this area.
